title: How Lovable self-improves every hour — Benjamin Verbeek, Lovable
talk_summary: Lovable mines production agent sessions for 'stuck' moments (repeated asks, complaints, abandoned sessions), extracts the eventual solution, clusters them into a curated 'Stack Overflow' knowledge bank injected by a lightweight model, and A/B-tests each entry's usefulness in production. Separately, they give the agent a 'vent' tool to report platform/tooling friction directly to Slack, which an agent triages into PRs.

takeaways.technique: Stuck-to-solved knowledge mining with production A/B gating
takeaways.what_they_do: An LLM judge flags sessions where users are stuck; when a session later succeeds, they extract what should have been injected at the start, cluster similar issues, and have an agent eval the entry against the original examples before adding it to a knowledge bank. A lightweight model injects entries when relevant, and a random holdout measures whether injected projects succeed more.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we inject a blank. So, we don't actually send anything for a small sample of use cases. And this allows us to with very high signal review whether this solution was actually useful in production.
takeaways.numbers: claims 'number of messages with fixing tent or people being stuck is dropping significantly' and more deploys; no hard figures

takeaways.technique: Aggressive staleness pruning of injected knowledge
takeaways.what_they_do: They continuously rebalance and delete knowledge entries because they go stale when models or features change, explicitly to avoid context rot.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It gets stale whenever a new model is released... we also have to throw away a lot of this context... not have a lot of old deprecated knowledge that is giving context rot

takeaways.technique: Agent 'vent' tool for platform friction, triaged by an agent into PRs
takeaways.what_they_do: The working agent gets a tool to report tooling/docs/platform problems it hit, sent to Slack; later an agent dedupes, investigates, and opens PRs, with humans reviewing/merging. Spikes in vents double as incident detection.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we actually have an agent that's monitoring removing duplicates and investigating and creating a PR for all these issues all the time
takeaways.numbers: '20 complaints about this in the first hour' for one filename bug

takeaways.what_they_do: Any injected context is randomly withheld for a small sample and outcomes compared between injected and withheld groups; entries that don't help are shown less or dropped.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We compare the the group of projects where it was injected and where we it could have been injected, but it wasn't

takeaways.technique: Cheap external reviewer instead of frontier model for monitoring
takeaways.what_they_do: They deliberately use a cheaper model as the external reviewer scanning lots of context, reserving frontier intelligence for the main work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You generally don't want top frontier level intelligence to look through a lot of context. But if it's in line, it's very very cheap comparatively.

takeaways.technique: Self-generated improvement backlog from agent feedback
takeaways.what_they_do: Agent-reported friction becomes an automated stream of small fix PRs, keeping a continuous supply of small, well-scoped work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: detecting a shortcoming, merging a fix, and then continuously review and eval that
